papers.title: When Covariates Mask Pre-Trends
papers.abstract: Honest difference-in-differences methods judge how far parallel trends may fail after treatment by how far it failed before treatment, as shown by placebo estimates. When the design adjusts for covariates, the placebo estimates are adjusted too. We show that this benchmark is valid only if the covariates are measured before the earliest placebo window. A covariate measured later already reflects shocks to the outcome during the placebo period, so adjusting for it hides part of the pre-trend. The placebos then look flatter than the true trend and the resulting confidence sets are too narrow. When the covariate is also observed at an early date, the distortion can be estimated and tested. Of 90 recent published studies that adjust for time-varying covariates, 77 measure at least one covariate too late.

papers.title: Sharp Fréchet--Hoeffding Bounds under Selectively Incomplete Observation
papers.abstract: Incomplete records can sharpen bounds on joint outcome probabilities even when no pair of outcomes is jointly observed. I derive sharp pointwise Fréchet--Hoeffding bounds combining known population marginals with selectively observed records, without restricting the observation mechanism. I establish an exact reduction of the identification problem to finite-dimensional optimization, yielding computable characterizations of both bounds. Illustrations involving income mobility, potential outcomes, and split questionnaires demonstrate how incomplete records can improve identification relative to the classical bounds.

papers.title: Coupling cellular trajectories and RNA kinetics on continuous expression manifolds with ManifoldVelo
papers.abstract: Jointly recovering pseudotime and RNA velocity from static single-cell transcriptomes requires reconciling global trajectory structure with local expression changes, particularly in complex cycles and branching differentiation. Here we introduce ManifoldVelo, a topology-conditioned framework that jointly learns cellular coordinates, continuous RNA trajectories and regulatory kinetics. Derivatives of unspliced and spliced RNA trajectories are matched to transcription-splicing-degradation dynamics, including between observed cells, allowing expression reconstruction, cellular ordering and kinetic estimation to inform one another. ManifoldVelo recovers pseudotime across all evaluated single-cell trajectory types, including cyclic, multibranch and smooth non-branching trajectories. ManifoldVelo achieves the best pseudotime recovery among compared methods in multipeak cyclic simulations and the highest directional agreement for spliced RNA velocity in both multipeak cyclic and branching simulations. Real-data analyses support phase prediction across experimental plates and differentiation trajectories consistent with pancreatic developmental stages and marker expression. Its central advantage is the joint recovery of temporal position and local dynamics across distinct trajectory structures within a reusable dynamic reference. New cells are assigned pseudotime and velocity predictions from spliced RNA alone, without refitting the reference model. ManifoldVelo provides a foundation for dynamic cell atlases that transfer learned temporal and kinetic information to new samples.

papers.title: Hybrid Federated Learning for Multimodal Fusion under Missing Modalities and Site Heterogeneity
papers.abstract: Multimodal fusion is studied under hybrid federation, where data are partitioned across samples and feature blocks. The proposed two-dimensional federated smooth multiple-kernel large-margin learning method (2D-FedSMKL) integrates availability-corrected modality scores, group-kernel regularization, and smooth worst-site risk aggregation. For fixed maps and propensities, the objective is convex and smooth. Curvature bounds and exact synchronous block-gradient equivalence are established for binary and multiclass scores, giving a conditional accelerated rate. An oracle-propensity binary risk bound and a propensity-perturbation result are also derived. Simulations and two public activity-recognition benchmarks assess site heterogeneity and modality absence. Worst-site aggregation improves worst-site performance under heterogeneity, including reversed and size-balanced designs. On the benchmarks, validation selects the correction; the selected model is not significantly worse than the strongest reference at the worst site, and group-regularization benefits vary by dataset.

papers.title: Features Extraction Across Multi-Source Heterogeneous Data
papers.abstract: High-dimensional data from multiple sources often combine shared structure with source-specific variation. We study heterogeneous principal component analysis, which seeks to recover common and private principal subspaces when their dimensions are unknown. {We propose \emph{Feature Extraction (FE)}, a novel data-driven framework with two steps. First, the Eigenvector-based Spike-Count (ESC) estimator determines the number of principal components (PC) in each source using only sample eigenvector information, rather than eigenvalue-based criteria. Second, FE identifies the locations of common features by comparing bias-corrected inner products between sample eigenvectors across sources. These matches yield estimates of the common and source-specific subspaces without iterative optimization. We establish the consistency of our estimators under a spiked covariance model in a high-dimensional regime where the dimension and sample size grow proportionally. Simulations and applications to federated image data and U.S. housing prices demonstrate the performance of FE in rank recovery, subspace estimation, and data reconstruction.} Code is available at https://github.com/liwenbo-research/HeterogeneousPCA

papers.title: Differentially Private Confidence Intervals for Relative Risk and Odds Ratio
papers.abstract: Ratio statistics, such as relative risk and odds ratio, are central tools for comparing outcome probabilities across populations, particularly in clinical and epidemiological studies. However, when the underlying counts are released under differential privacy, the resulting ratio estimators can exhibit nontrivial bias and variance, and principled methods for statistical inference in this setting remain limited. In this work, we study estimation and inference for ratio statistics computed from counts perturbed by additive Laplace or Gaussian noise. We show that the natural plug-in estimators based on privatized counts are consistent, and we derive confidence intervals that explicitly account for both sampling variability and privacy-induced noise, making our approach appealing for moderate sample sizes. Our analysis provides transparent variance decompositions that clarify when privacy meaningfully affects inference. Empirical results on simulated and real datasets demonstrate that, for moderate privacy levels and sample sizes, the proposed confidence intervals closely match their non-private counterparts, while properly reflecting additional uncertainty in small-sample regimes. Our results provide both theoretical guarantees and practical guidance for conducting statistical inference with ratio statistics under differential privacy.

papers.title: One-Sample Mendelian Randomization and Instrumental Variable Analyses in R and Stata: The OneSampleMR and ivonesamplemr Packages
papers.abstract: Mendelian randomization (MR) uses genetic variants as instrumental variables (IVs) to estimate the causal effect of an exposure on an outcome. When individual-level data on the instruments, exposure, and outcome are available in a single sample (one-sample MR), a range of IV estimators can be used beyond the standard two-stage least squares estimator, including structural mean models (SMMs) and two-stage predictor substitu- tion (TSPS) and two-stage residual inclusion (TSRI) estimators with nonlinear second stage models. These estimators are important when the outcome is binary, where in- vestigators typically wish to report causal risk ratios or causal odds ratios. However, implementations of these estimators are scattered across software packages and are of- ten unavailable with standard errors that account for the estimation of the first stage. We describe two packages which implement these estimators: OneSampleMR for R and ivonesamplemr for Stata. Both packages fit the multiplicative and logistic SMMs and TSPS and TSRI estimators with identity, log-additive, log-multiplicative, and logit links using the generalized method of moments (GMM), so that the standard errors account for the uncertainty in both stages of estimation. OneSampleMR additionally provides the Sanderson-Windmeijer conditional F-statistic for assessing instrument strength in models with multiple exposures, and ivonesamplemr additionally provides prefix commands for moving window and within-quantile estimation for exploring nonlinear exposure-outcome relationships. We illustrate both packages using the same simulated dataset and show that they give the same estimates as each other and as existing implementations.

papers.title: Conditional expectile-based value-at-risk: Semiparametric estimation and inference
papers.abstract: Conditional expectile-based value-at-risk (EVaR) has attracted increasing attention in financial risk management owing to its desirable theoretical properties. However, existing estimation methods for conditional EVaR either rely on potentially misspecified parametric models or suffer from the curse of dimensionality in nonparametric approaches. To this end, we study semiparametric estimation and inference for conditional EVaR in nonlinear time series models with unspecified error distribution. Specifically, we propose a two-step conditional EVaR estimator that achieves the parametric convergence rate. Furthermore, we derive a functional central limit theorem for conditional EVaR process, and then extend to investigate estimating both conditional expectile-based expected shortfall and conditional distribution. A residual bootstrap procedure is proposed for non-expert practitioners to conduct statistical inference. The asymptotic results and their applications are illustrated by numerical studies and an empirical application to S\&P 500 returns.

papers.title: A Bayesian quantile mixed model for bounded discrete outcomes
papers.abstract: Quantile regression for longitudinal bounded integer outcomes must accommodate discreteness, finite support, and dependence within participants. We develop a Bayesian quantile mixed model using a discrete Kumaraswamy distribution parameterized through a smooth quantile anchor whose ceiling gives the corresponding integer quantile. Covariates and correlated Gaussian participant effects enter a logit predictor for the scaled anchor, while a separate regression models distributional shape. Posterior computation combines a conjugate Gaussian coefficient update, available for compatible fixed and random effect designs, with slice sampling and covariance interweaving. Simulations showed small biases in regression coefficients and generally near-nominal coverage of 95% credible intervals. An application to repeated cognitive scores illustrates covariate associations across separately fitted quantile levels. Posterior predictive checks captured broad distributional patterns.

papers.title: HistoTx: Early fusion of H&E images and spatial transcriptomics at varying spatial transcriptomics resolution with self-supervised learning
papers.abstract: Spatial transcriptomics maps gene expression across tissue sections and, when integrated with whole slide images, jointly captures both morphological architecture and molecular activity to provide a rich, multimodal view of tissue biology. ML approaches combining spatial transcriptomics and WSIs typically learn a mapping from morphological features to molecular profiles via contrastive alignment or supervised fine-tuning of pathology foundation models. In both cases, transcriptomics serves as a training signal rather than a true input modality, leaving inference fundamentally image-driven. We propose an early-fusion vision transformer architecture in which transcript tokens are constructed at arbitrary spatial resolution, merged with image patch tokens, and jointly processed through a shared transformer stack for deep cross-modal interaction. Starting from a pretrained vision-only pathology foundation model, we train HistoTx by continuing self-supervised pretraining on paired image and spatial transcriptomics data and demonstrate that: 1) at inference with image only, performance remains on par with the baseline on most tasks while improving on tasks that inherently benefit from molecular knowledge, such as gene expression prediction; 2) when both modalities are available at inference, jointly providing image and transcript inputs outperforms either modality alone.

papers.title: Improving the selection-function-based sensitivity analysis for publication bias with restricted maximum likelihood
papers.abstract: In random-effects meta-analysis, the between-study variance quantifies the heterogeneity among studies. Without selective publication, the restricted maximum likelihood (REML) method is recommended for this variance, since the maximum likelihood (ML) method underestimates it when the number of studies is small. However, under selective publication, referred to as publication bias (PB), the published studies no longer follow the normal-normal model, and the REML cannot be directly applied. Thus, the existing sensitivity analysis methods for PB based on selection functions estimate the between-study variance by the ML conditional on published studies and inherit its underestimation. This underestimation also affects the estimate of the common effect and its confidence interval. To improve the estimation of the common effect and the heterogeneity, we propose a REML-type estimator of the between-study variance for the selection-function-based sensitivity analysis. It centers the profile score by its approximate mean and reduces exactly to the REML without PB. The proposed sensitivity analysis method is a more accurate alternative to the ML-based sensitivity analysis in meta-analyses with a small number of studies, and it is the first REML-type estimator in the presence of PB. Simulation studies substantiate that the proposed method reduces the median bias of the between-study variance and improves the estimation error and coverage probability for the common effect compared with the conditional ML. We illustrate the proposed method with two meta-analyses on high maintenance-dose clopidogrel and nicotine gum for smoking cessation. The proposed method would give useful guidance on the between-study heterogeneity in sensitivity analysis for PB.

papers.title: Reference-based sensitivity analysis for bounded longitudinal outcomes
papers.abstract: Reference-based sensitivity analysis is widely used to assess departures from the assumption that data are missing at random in longitudinal randomized trials, but existing methods are typically formulated for approximately Gaussian continuous outcomes and do not directly accommodate bounded outcomes, particularly when exact lower or upper bounds may occur with appreciable probability. We propose a Bayesian reference-based sensitivity analysis framework for bounded longitudinal outcomes, based on a thresholded latent Gaussian working model. Interior observations are mapped one-to-one to the latent scale, whereas boundary observations correspond to latent values below or above prespecified thresholds, yielding a distribution on the observed scale with a continuous interior density and positive mass at the bounds. Reference-based rules are imposed on the latent scale, and posterior predictive imputation proceeds on that scale before mapping back to the original outcome scale. Simulations assessed model calibration, recovery of complete data contrasts, and population treatment effect inference after imputation. For the proposed model, population treatment effect inference showed small bias when the analysis rule matched the truth rule after the trigger, but conservative Rubin intervals, particularly under jump to reference. The method is illustrated using the BtheB study, a longitudinal trial with a bounded depression outcome and incomplete follow-up.

papers.title: Where Is a Prediction Model Miscalibrated, and for Whom? Local Audits in Outcome-Learned Pockets
papers.abstract: Overall and group-level averages, and ranking metrics such as the AUC, can hide sets of observations for which a prediction model systematically over- or under-predicts. We present an audit that asks where a model is miscalibrated (in which sets of similar observations it over- or under-predicts on average) and for whom (whether its average prediction error differs between demographic groups, such as by race or sex, within the same set). It groups observations into pockets using random-forest similarity, which weighs each feature by its importance for predicting the outcome, with a ridge-regression grouping alongside. Pockets are learned on one sample and tested on another, with simultaneous confidence intervals that allow for correlation within units such as hospitals; the audit needs only features, outcomes and fixed predictions. In 17 simulation scenarios with an error planted for one group, the combined audit located it better than the strongest alternative grouping in 15, with false-alarm rates near or below 5%; with a local error planted for everyone, it won in 12 of 15 scenarios at the smaller error size and lost when the error was unrelated to the outcome. In public synthetic data from the care-management algorithm studied by Obermeyer et al., it found no detectable overall error but under-prediction of illness in the sickest pockets and over-prediction elsewhere, and distinguished Black patients' concentration where the score under-predicted for everyone from a Black-White gap within pockets. For APACHE IVa, an exploratory analysis located its previously reported over-prediction of ICU mortality in a mostly ventilated pocket and a low-risk pocket, with none detected in a moderate-risk one. Two chest X-ray classifiers showed offsetting local errors behind no detectable overall error. Code: https://github.com/modenesi/pocket-audit

papers.title: Exact Simes inequalities for two-sided Gaussian tests
papers.abstract: The Simes test combines marginal p-values to test a global null hypothesis. Whether it controls the type I error for two-sided Gaussian tests with arbitrary covariance remains open. We prove that, for every fixed number $m$ of tests, the rejection probability does not exceed the nominal level when that level is sufficiently small. The same range of levels works for every covariance matrix. Equality holds if and only if the p-values form independent groups with identical values within each group. For $m=3$, a computer-assisted proof establishes validity at $0.05$, and an analytic argument extends it to an explicit interval around $0.05$. As the number $m$ of tests increases, we prove validity in two settings: each test statistic is correlated with at most a fixed number of others; or the statistics form independent blocks whose sizes grow sufficiently slowly, at a specified rate of order $\log\log m$. Both settings allow arbitrary correlations within these restrictions. For any fixed $0<a<1$, validity holds for every $m$ above a threshold $M$ and every level $0<α\le a$; the same $M$ works for all allowed covariances. Further results quantify the difference between the nominal level and the rejection probability, and permit more correlated neighbors when their correlations are bounded away from $\pm1$. We do not obtain numerical values for the general small-level cutoffs or the required number of tests.

papers.title: Joint Estimation and Grouping of Quantile Association Curves across Multiple Responses
papers.abstract: Large biobanks provide an opportunity to study how associations with related traits vary across age and across their distributions. We propose a quantile regression procedure that jointly groups responses and estimates their shared varying-coefficient curves on conditional percentile scales. An information criterion selects both the number of groups and their membership from grouped B-spline fits. We establish consistent group recovery, curve convergence rates, and feasible pointwise inference after group selection as the spline dimension grows. The analysis distinguishes true curve differences from improvements due to separate spline approximations of a shared curve. Errors in the estimated percentile scales partly cancel in comparisons of pooled and split fits of a shared curve, but can still contribute to the asymptotic variance of the curve estimators. In 127,040 UK Biobank women aged 40 to 70, we grouped nine metabolic traits by their associations with a type 2 diabetes polygenic risk score and found seven groups at the median, compared with three and four at the lower and upper quantiles. The method identifies shared tail associations among traits with distinct median associations, allowing their information to be pooled where the curves agree.

papers.title: Selective Randomization Inference for Interference
papers.abstract: Empirical researchers often use tests for interference as pretests or robustness checks. However, when the results guide the choice of models, parameters, or hypotheses, the resulting data-dependent selection can compromise the validity of subsequent inference. This paper develops a two-stage selective randomization inference framework for interference that explicitly conditions on the selection event to account for data-dependent selection. We first test the null hypothesis of no treatment spillover using a conditional randomization method. If this null is rejected, we test the null hypothesis of zero exposure contrast under a pre-specified exposure mapping that allows for spillover effects; otherwise, we test the null hypothesis of no direct effects under the assumption of no spillover. We prove that each second-stage test controls the selective Type I error rate in finite samples and evaluate the size and power of the proposed tests through Monte Carlo experiments.

papers.title: Diagnosing Model--Item Interactions in Language Model Benchmarks with LSIRM
papers.abstract: Language models with similar benchmark accuracy can succeed on different items. Overall scores do not show where their performance differs or which item properties might explain those differences. We demonstrate how the latent space item response model (LSIRM) can help evaluators investigate these patterns and their consequences for model comparison. We analyze 1,348 language models on 5,761 BBH items and compare ways of presenting and scoring answers across BBH, GPQA, MMLU-Pro, and MuSR. We examine LSIRM maps, which summarize differences in performance across models and items, alongside item properties and records of correct and incorrect responses. In BBH, nearby items on these maps often share the same correct answer, such as "Yes" or "No." Across the four benchmarks, this pattern is stronger when answers are scored using option labels, such as A, B, C, and D, than when using the text of the options. We then estimate each model's tendency to perform better or worse on items with particular correct answers and quantify how this tendency contributes to its score. This separates an estimated contribution associated with correct answers from the remaining differences in item performance. Two models' total numbers of correct answers differed by only 14 out of 5,761 items. Excluding the estimated answer-category contribution from their scores moved their ranks hundreds of places in opposite directions, while keeping all other estimates unchanged. The approach helps evaluators identify differences hidden by overall accuracy and understand how the choice of what to include in a score affects model rankings.

papers.title: A Scientific Claim Stability Framework for Evaluating MRI Morphometry Pipelines
papers.abstract: MRI morphometry pipelines are often evaluated by measurement agreement or downstream accuracy, yet their scientific value depends on the conclusions they support. Two pipelines can produce similar feature-level results yet support different conclusions about aging, cognitive decline, or neurodegeneration. We introduce Scientific Claim Stability (SCS), a claim-centric evaluation framework that converts region-of-interest (ROI) morphometry tables into auditable claim cards and evaluates their support under changes in dataset, processing pipeline, atlas, feature family, and target. Across 10,370 MRI scans from three datasets and five cohorts, SCS generates 2,783 claim cards and evaluates 89 claim-family pairs. The evaluation distinguishes stable, transferable, and fragile claims. FreeSurfer 8-FastSurfer comparisons show high evidence concordance and low anatomical-support overlap under the primary covariate specification. Acquisition-adjusted analyses show that the magnitude of support disagreement depends on the model specification. Structured review by specialists in geriatrics, neuroscience, and radiology, alongside auxiliary ChatGPT and Gemini reviewers, assesses claim plausibility, clarity, faithfulness, usefulness, and caution. SCS provides a reproducible way to audit the evidential stability of morphometry claims without assuming a universal gold standard.

papers.title: Attribution-based diagnostics for single-cell foundation models
papers.abstract: Single-cell RNA foundation models (scFMs) are increasingly used for in-silico biological discovery, yet predictive performance alone does not reveal whether their decisions rely on biologically meaningful signals or model-specific shortcuts. We systematically investigate post-hoc attribution of downstream predictions across two tasks: cell-type annotation using pretrained Cell2Sentence and scGPT models, and perturbation prediction using scGPT+STATE in a controlled setting. For cell annotation, we use attribution to assess whether predictions rely on established marker genes and how their relevance varies with model architecture, expression rank, and the surrounding cellular context. For perturbation prediction, we compare attribution patterns with known regulatory ground-truth in a synthetic setting to assess what they reveal about the model's learned computations. Across these tasks, attribution reveals biological feature use, contextual interactions, contributions from different input pathways, learning progression, associations with prediction quality, and potential pitfalls that are not fully captured by standard performance metrics. Experiments with complete and limited regulatory knowledge further demonstrate that conclusions drawn from attribution depend strongly on the choice of biological reference, baseline, and null model. Together, these findings highlight the value of attribution as a flexible post-hoc diagnostic for understanding model behavior, identifying potential issues, and informing the development of scFMs.

papers.title: The DynaCell Evaluation Suite for Dynamic 3D Virtual Staining of Live Cells
papers.abstract: Understanding how cells respond to perturbations over time is central to cell biology and drug discovery. Live-cell imaging captures the dynamics of perturbation-induced phenotypes in individual cells. While fluorescence imaging can visualize specific molecular phenotypes, labeling and repeated illumination often affect cell health. Virtual staining offers an alternative by predicting these fluorescence images from images acquired without fluorescent labels. Although many virtual staining models have been developed, their performance on volumetric time-lapse data remains poorly characterized. We address this gap with an evaluation suite for 3D time-lapse virtual staining of live cells. The suite combines paired 3D time-lapse images acquired with and without fluorescent labels, a set of baseline models, and three metric tiers measuring pixel-level fidelity, organelle segmentation performance, and single-cell phenotype similarity. Using this evaluation suite, we study metric and model behavior across 3 cell types, 2 microscopes, 4 organelles, and 3 perturbation states. We find that regression baselines better predict the spatial localization of target organelles, whereas the generative baseline better captures the distribution of phenotypes across cells. These differences expose trade-offs between structural and phenotypic fidelity that are obscured by single-metric evaluation and suggest how virtual staining models can be developed for diverse downstream tasks such as localization, segmentation, tracking, and phenotypic profiling. We release the curated datasets, baseline checkpoints, and evaluation code as part of DynaCell, a broader framework for image-based profiling of cell-state dynamics.

papers.title: Metric Subtraction for Non-Euclidean Random Objects with Applications to Residual Analysis
papers.abstract: Residual analysis for non-Euclidean regression models is challenging due to the lack of a natural subtraction operation and a corresponding notion of conditionally centered residuals. We introduce a metric subtraction framework that yields residuals in the original response space, with their conditional Fréchet mean equal to a fixed reference object when the model is correctly specified. We establish sufficient conditions for this conditional centering property, together with a separate condition ensuring distance preservation, providing a construction principle for suitable metric subtraction operators. The proposed metric subtraction framework accommodates several important classes of metric spaces, including spheres, symmetric positive definite matrices, simplices, and Wasserstein spaces. Building on this framework, we develop a randomized test for detecting remaining conditional location effects and establish its asymptotic size and power against fixed alternatives. We further introduce two complementary diagnostic tools, signed distance plots and distance-profile-based boxplots, to visualize systematic residual patterns and identify atypical observations. For uncertainty quantification, we construct residual-based prediction sets and establish their asymptotic validity. Simulation studies and applications to New York City bicycle usage distributions and U.S. electricity generation compositions demonstrate the practical utility of the proposed framework for model assessment, residual diagnostics, and prediction in non-Euclidean regression.

papers.title: Partial Invariance for Classification under Structural Causal Models
papers.abstract: Making predictions in an unseen environment from data collected across multiple training environments is challenging. This challenge is particularly pronounced when the target-generating mechanism varies across environments. In this work, we introduce environment-label separation, a form of partial environmental invariance that decomposes the target conditional distribution into an environment-invariant component and a label-invariant component. We show that this partial invariance enables estimation of the target conditional distribution in an unseen environment when using labeled training data together with unlabeled test features. Within the structural causal model framework, we provide sufficient conditions for environment-label separation. Building on these conditions, we develop an algorithm, dIMP-Classifier, which jointly minimizes an estimate of the test risk and encourages invariance across environments. We further provide finite-sample guarantees that characterize the test risk in terms of deviations from invariance, estimation error, and sample complexity. Experiments on simulated data and the real-world light tunnel Causal Chamber data demonstrate that the proposed approach can perform under interventions on the target mechanism and consistently outperforms the considered standard and invariance-based baselines.

papers.title: A General Approach for Assessing Sensitivity to Violations of Causal Assumptions
papers.abstract: Although causal sensitivity analyses are widely used to assess the robustness of conclusions, a key limitation is that existing methods are typically developed for specific designs. This paper develops a general sensitivity analysis framework that applies to a wide range of discrete causal models and estimands by deriving sharp bounds on causal estimands as a function of the maximum proportion of the population for which the assumption is relaxed. The framework is built on the generalized principal strata approach, which allows the translation of assumptions, estimands, and data into polynomial programs. In this approach, three classes of assumptions can be relaxed: a) functional restrictions, which limit the ways that one variable can respond to another, e.g. strong monotonicity; b) exclusion restrictions, which rule out direct causal effects; c) unconfoundedness, which rules out unobserved common causes of variables. The approach produces both sharp sensitivity curves and robustness values, i.e., the smallest sensitivity level at which the sign of a causal effect stops being identified. The applicability of the method is demonstrated by generalizing existing proportion-of-violations approaches, deriving new sensitivity analysis methods for instrumental variable and selection-on-observables designs, and reanalyzing empirical results.

papers.title: Empirical rather than simulated spectral band adjustment of MODIS to Sentinel-3 OLCI for European vegetation monitoring
papers.abstract: Spectral band adjustment derived from convolved spectra describes sensor differences under controlled conditions, but its applicability to operational products requires assessment. We compare this approach with adjustment estimated directly from MODIS and Sentinel-3 OLCI observations for European vegetation monitoring. Both streams undergo atmospheric correction and Ross-Thick/Li-Sparse Reciprocal BRDF normalization to nadir viewing and local solar noon. Using observations from 2019-2024, we derive annual OLCI/MODIS reflectance-ratio relationships with unadjusted MODIS NDVI. The operational correction uses quadratic red and linear near-infrared (NIR) functions. We compare these relationships with irradiance-weighted canopy simulations and assess the empirical correction at 460 locations. Simulated and empirical relationships differ, particularly for red reflectance at high NDVI. Background-dependent simulated ratios also demonstrate the limitations of a single NDVI-based function. The empirical correction reduces red and NIR root-mean-square error (RMSE) at 66.3% and 71.1% of locations, with median paired reductions of 5.98% and 13.67%. Median paired RMSE decreases by 0.86% for NDVI but increases by 0.95% for EVI2, 0.74% for NIRv and 7.07% for the Plant Phenology Index (PPI), calculated with stream-specific historical references. This study establishes an operational empirical adjustment and shows that the specified spectral simulation does not reproduce the relationship between the normalized products. It provides evidence for improved reflectance consistency while demonstrating that vegetation-index benefits require separate assessment.

papers.title: Directional Nonlinear Principal Components: a measure transportation approach
papers.abstract: One of the earliest techniques in multivariate analysis, Principal Component Analysis (PCA) remains among the most popular ones in the area. PCA, however, is a linear and bidirectional technique (principal directions $\pm\mathbf{u}$ are defined up to a sign), which is fine under Gaussian or elliptical assumptions but constitutes a major limitation outside that restrictive context. This has prompted the development of numerous nonlinear approaches. We show here how recent results in measure transportation allow for a nonlinear and strictly directional (disentangling $\mathbf{u}$ and $-\mathbf{u}$) concept preserving the intuitive interpretation of the classical linear concept by maximizing expected squared arc lengths along data-driven principal curves rather than principal directions.

papers.title: A multivariate unsupervised lognormal-GPD mixture for dependent losses
papers.abstract: We propose a multivariate two-population mixture distribution for heavy-tailed and positively skewed non-negative data. The first mixture population is a multivariate lognormal, while the second is a distribution obtained by joining univariate zero-mean generalized Pareto densities via a Gumbel copula. The model is unsupervised, since no threshold has to be set or estimated. We derive some properties of the distribution and develop an Expectation-Conditional Maximization algorithm for maximum likelihood estimation, which is found to perform well in multivariate contexts beyond the bivariate case. The finite-sample properties of the estimators are assessed by means of simulation experiments, and an empirical application to aggregated commercial property-casualty insurance claims illustrates the impact of dependence on risk estimation. All the methods are implemented in the R package MultLognGPD, available on Github.

papers.title: Optimal spectral shrinkage via Krylov approximation
papers.abstract: Spectral shrinkage encompasses a broad family of estimators for high-dimensional linear regression that regularize estimation and prediction by applying spectral filters to the sample covariance matrix. Despite its widespread use, achieving oracle-optimal prediction risk under general covariance structures remains challenging, as the oracle filter requires unknown population quantities and has a closed form only for specific covariance models such as isotropic and spiked models. We propose \textit{risk-targeted Krylov fitting} (RTK), a data-driven spectral estimator that adapts to the unknown covariance structure and attains the oracle risk asymptotically. Like partial least squares, RTK operates in an $m$-dimensional Krylov space, but it targets the oracle risk directly by minimizing the leave-one-out risk, which we compute exactly without refitting the model $n$ times. Under general distributions and covariance structures, RTK attains the optimal prediction risk in the Krylov space up to $O(1/n)$. Furthermore, its risk approaches that of the optimal analytic filter with $m$ of order $\log n$. In simulations over a wide range of covariance structures, RTK and a truncated variant were robust to the choice of $m$ and consistently among the spectral estimators closest to the oracle. In applications to single-cell sequencing data and large-scale neural recordings, the proposed methods achieved higher prediction accuracy than competing estimators on most tasks.

papers.title: Looking Forward to Constructing Better Causal Comparisons
papers.abstract: Constructing credible comparison groups is a central challenge in observational causal inference. Conventional approaches assess comparability through observed characteristics or pre-treatment outcome trajectories, although causal identification depends on unobserved untreated potential outcomes after treatment. We propose a forward-looking framework that selects or weights controls using prognostic scores: predictions, based on pre-treatment information, of the outcomes units would experience without treatment. These scores target either untreated outcome levels or changes, depending on the comparability condition underlying the causal design. They can be estimated using post-treatment outcomes observed for untreated units or exclusively from historical data. To construct these scores, we leverage tabular foundation models, whose extensive pretraining enables them to capture complex relationships among predictors and effectively extract their predictive information, even when application-specific samples are limited. Crucially, predictions guide comparison-group construction, whereas observed outcomes determine treatment effect estimates. We derive an exact decomposition of estimation error into prognostic-score imbalance and differences in forecast errors, clarifying why neither predictive accuracy nor score balance alone guarantees causal identification. The National Supported Work application reveals that stronger pre-treatment covariate balance does not necessarily yield estimates closer to experimental benchmarks, highlighting the practical relevance of prognostic-score comparisons.

papers.title: Minimax-Optimal Static Estimators Under Interference
papers.abstract: We study the problem of estimating the global treatment effect in randomized experiments under interference, where a unit's outcome may depend on the treatment assignments of other units. We adopt a minimax framework, allowing an adversary to select an outcome function from a class of functions that satisfy bounded outcomes and bounded interference. We derive minimax-optimal static estimators that are robust to a wide range of interference structures, parameterized by a scalar $δ$ controlling the maximum influence of one unit's treatment on another's outcome. Under large interference, we observe two regimes. When the treatment and control groups are equally sized, the minimax-optimal static estimator is the zero estimator. When one of the two groups is larger, the minimax-optimal static estimator is a "half-zero" estimator, in which the outcomes of the smaller group are ignored, and the estimator only considers the outcomes of the larger group.

papers.title: Does Calibration Pick the Right Model? Likelihood Evidence from Income Risk
papers.abstract: Quantitative macroeconomics typically disciplines models by matching selected moments. We show how finite-state hidden Markov approximations make likelihood estimation and model selection feasible for nonlinear, non-Gaussian latent processes on short panels, without simulation. We illustrate the method with PSID earnings data. The calibrations that best match moments of earnings dynamics fit complete histories worse than a likelihood-estimated process with a Gaussian persistent component. In a standard saving model, calibrations of one process that fit the targets about equally well imply mean assets that differ by a factor of three. Close agreement with selected moments can leave economic predictions largely undetermined.

papers.title: Randomized Adaptive Sequential Allocation and the Limits of Bounded Exposure to Inferior Treatments
papers.abstract: A clinical trial must learn which treatment is superior while sparing its participants from the inferior one. Kundu et al. 2025 recently showed that a purely deterministic rule, which always assigns the treatment with the larger current sample mean, achieves a strong form of this ethical goal. The smaller allocation count stays almost surely finite and has all moments bounded uniformly in the sample size. Deterministic allocation is, however, predictable, and predictability invites selection bias. We ask whether this bounded-exposure phenomenon survives once the deterministic rule is replaced by a smooth randomized one. We show that it does not. Under any fixed non-degenerate symmetric randomization, both treatments are sampled infinitely often, the adaptive sample means are strongly consistent, and the inferior treatment draws a strictly positive limiting allocation proportion. Consequently, the inferior allocation count grows linearly and its moments are unbounded. We then study annealed randomization, in which the randomization scale cools with the accumulated information, and obtain summability and divergence criteria that separate finite, sublinear, and linear exposure. A forced-exploration variant identifies the superior treatment with probability one while keeping the inferior exposure sublinear, and thereby frees the annealed guarantees from any correct-stabilization event. We also treat normalized multi-treatment rules, ties, indifference zones, unequal variances, general response distributions, and local alternatives. Finally, we develop the post-trial asymptotic inference that each exposure regime permits. The results delineate the trade-off between allocation concealment, persistent exploration, and ethical concentration on the superior treatment.

papers.title: The precision of fractional factorial designs under randomization
papers.abstract: A regular fraction of a two-level factorial design runs fewer treatment combinations (cells), with more units in each. With the number of units fixed, more units per cell do not by themselves reduce the variance. Averaged over the fractions of one defining contrast subgroup, a fraction's variance is smaller than the full design's by the unit-to-unit variation of the aliased effects, a gain the usual variance estimator misses. Assuming the aliased effects are zero, we propose a full-design estimator that weights the fractions' contrasts by inverse variance. Its estimated variance never exceeds the saturated estimator's. In large samples, it is proportional to the harmonic mean of the fractions' average cell variances, and a fraction's, on average, to the arithmetic mean. We test this assumption, but choosing between the two estimators by the test can lose coverage. The results extend to unequal allocations, and the large-sample results to covariate adjustment.

papers.title: Inference for conditional Fréchet means via Riemannian Robust Bias Correction
papers.abstract: We develop an intrinsic framework for inference on conditional Fréchet means with predictors and responses taking values in finite-dimensional Riemannian manifolds. We derive a second-order expansion of the smoothing bias, represented in the tangent space via the logarithm map, and show that this bias can affect first-order inference. We propose Riemannian robust bias correction (RRBC), which estimates the leading smoothing bias using a local quadratic regression in the response tangent space and corrects the estimator through the exponential map. Our leave-one-out (LOO) covariance estimator uses intrinsic displacements between the full-sample and LOO RRBC estimates, accounting for the variability of the estimated bias correction and its covariance with the local linear estimator. We establish asymptotically valid pointwise confidence sets and simultaneous confidence tubes without undersmoothing. Simulations on spheres and symmetric positive-definite matrices show that RRBC can improve coverage when smoothing bias is nonnegligible. Cardiovascular and ocean-current applications illustrate simultaneous hypothesis testing and inference for smooth functionals.

papers.title: Exploiting Locally Exogeneous Variation in Spatial Data: Linear Regression with Many Small Units
papers.abstract: This article shows how researchers can exploit \textit{locally exogeneous variation} even in the presence of endogeneity, autocorrelation, or spurious correlation. It describes the infill asymptotic properties of generalized least squares estimation with county-level data, Census tract-level data, and similar regional averages, including sufficient conditions for consistency, asymptotic normality, and valid inference.

papers.title: Testing Exogeneity in Nonparametric Instrumental Variable Models
papers.abstract: We propose a test of mean exogeneity in nonparametric instrumental variable models. Under completeness, the null is equivalent to a conditional moment restriction involving the ordinary regression function, so the test avoids estimation of the structural function and its ill-posed inverse problem. We construct a residual-marked empirical process and analyze it through an auxiliary U-process of order two. We derive its limiting distributions under the null and Pitman-type local alternatives of order $n^{-1/2}$, and establish consistency against fixed global alternatives. The analysis reveals a nonparametric estimation effect that invalidates a direct multiplier bootstrap. We propose a computationally simple multiplier bootstrap with a tailor-made indicator correction to account for this effect, and establish its asymptotic validity. Simulations show good size control and power gains over existing methods in the nonparametric designs considered. An application to a wage equation provides evidence against the mean exogeneity of schooling.

papers.title: Learning AI Agents, Market Makers, and Stress in Automated Markets
papers.abstract: Automated markets increasingly route order flow from learning trading agents through automated market makers (AMMs). We model trader archetypes as AI agents defined by their reward functions and analyze the feedback they create on a constant-product AMM. Herd-dominated and arbitrage-dominated markets of equal size have identical return distributions and turnover, so no rule based on volatility, value-at-risk, stress frequency, or volume can tell them apart; yet their stress episodes differ in length by a factor unbounded in the feedback-to-noise ratio $β/s$. Serial statistics identify the feedback sign from $Θ((s/β)^2\log(1/δ))$ observations, and this rate is tight. When agents trade together, profit-seeking agents ride herds rather than lean against them, leading to all-or-nothing participation. Spread-earning market makers restore stability but make liquidity fragile, with discontinuous collapse and hysteresis; maker--taker pricing, not a uniform fee, is the effective instrument.

papers.title: Searching for related contributors to a DNA mixture using single cell analysis
papers.abstract: We propose a staged process for assessing the presence of related individuals in an autosomal STR DNA mixture sample, when it is analysed using a single cell pipeline analysis (as opposed to a bulk mixture analysis). In the absence of a large dataset if single cells from real related people, artificial single cell data is generated by sampling individual locus data taken from single cell dataset of real unrelated people. It is applied to create random admixtures used in a relatedness search for pairs of individuals to illustrate the usefulness of the method.

papers.title: Graph-Based Testing of Conditional Mean Independence with Applications to Large Language Model Evaluation
papers.abstract: We study whether a predictor $X$ provides additional information for predicting a scalar response $Y$ after adjustment for other variables $Z$, formalized by testing $\mathsf{H}_0:\E(Y\mid X,Z)=\E(Y\mid Z)$. Existing methods often require estimating nuisance functions involving $X$, which can be difficult for high-dimensional or structured predictors. We propose a graph-based test that extends the edge count principle to covariate adjustment. It represents $X$ through pairwise dissimilarities, estimates only the baseline regression $\E(Y\mid Z)$, and aggregates products of held-out residuals across graph edges. We develop sample-splitting and two-fold cross-fitting versions. Under regularity conditions, both have standard normal null limits, yielding analytic $p$-values, and are consistent under graph-smooth and graph-rough alternatives. Simulations with vector, image, and network predictors show good size control and power advantages over competing procedures, with cross-fitting improving power across the main alternatives. Applications examine human quality ratings, mathematical error labels, and LLM response preferences. Our method detects associations with quality ratings and an LLM judge's preferences after adjustment for text length and other recorded characteristics.

papers.title: Comparative Strategies for Handling Imbalanced QSAR Regression: A Case Study on hERG Activity Prediction
papers.abstract: Data imbalance frequently occurs in QSAR modeling, yet most studies focus on classification tasks, and few address regression tasks, as it is challenging to determine which regions of the data are sparse or dense. Data-level and algorithm-level imbalance-handling strategies can have different effects on model performance. In this study, we systematically compare various strategies across GCN and fingerprint-based machine learning models. To evaluate model performance more meaningfully, we partitioned the target region into several subregions based on both domain knowledge and data distribution. We focused on the region of greatest practical interest. Our results demonstrate that selecting models based on this interest-region metric leads to more reliable performance than using the total region metric. We also observed that different imbalance-handling strategies can have divergent effects depending on the model type. These findings highlight the importance of region-aware evaluation in regression QSAR modeling and provide practical guidance for selecting appropriate strategies for imbalanced datasets.

papers.title: Stand-In Effects and Pooling Amplification: Design-Based Tests of Whether Biological World Models Use Actions
papers.abstract: Action-conditioned world models are increasingly trained on data from randomized experiments, and whether their predictions respond to actions is usually checked by replacing or removing the actions and measuring the loss in accuracy. We show that such diagnostics report action effects where there are none: under autocorrelated designs, future actions stand in for history the model does not see, and a better model learns the stand-in better. When the design law is known, a conditional randomization test written as an e-value is valid in finite samples whatever the model, provided the resampler conditions on the full state the design used; resampling from a simpler law reproduces the false effect. We identify a second failure, specific to world models: when many sites share one action sequence (cells in a microscope field, pixels in a frame), the natural pooled score turns small model errors along the action contrast into overwhelming evidence against a true effect. In a pixel world, its median log e-value fell from $-17.3$ to $-6832$ as frames grew from 64 to 4096 pixels, while the oracle's rose. Tempering the score by a design effect estimated on training data changes the bet, not the validity. Our own preregistered analysis of optogenetic ERK experiments failed in exactly this way; a tempered statistic, selected on synthetic data and registered before the data were obtained, then rejected the null on a never-opened field ($E\approx 1.1\times10^{10}$). Every analysis is preregistered, fixed in a dated protocol before it was run, or labelled exploratory, and every reported result is generated from hashed result files.

papers.title: Moment-Orthogonal Quadratic-Envelope E-Processes for Anytime-Valid Location Inference
papers.abstract: E-process confidence sequences for unbounded means typically use a variance bound and a first-order score, leaving skewness and kurtosis unused. We construct a quadratic-envelope e-process from a conditionally centered vector score with a predictable second-moment bound. Under moment information specified independently of the tested stream, it stays positive on unbounded support and gives exact anytime-valid coverage under predictable strategies and fixed mixtures, without score clipping. For a location family with known central moments through order four, the centered observation and its centered square yield an exact confidence sequence whose local width shrinks, relative to a first-order construction, by a factor determined by skewness and kurtosis. At level 5%, the largest null ever-crossing rate was 4.63%; on two zero-inflated-lognormal families median stopping times fell by 36.8-45.8%. When the moments are calibrated on an independent reference sample, a centering-robust factor keeps exact coverage at a closed-form width cost: the median gain was 21.6-30.3% for Gamma(2) and lognormal errors with 10^6 reference observations, and a loss of up to 9.9% with 10^4. On public Fermi gamma-ray detector data with a declared stability margin, it crossed at the current location in 1.8% of 225 windows and stopped 30-35% earlier than the calibrated first-order method.

papers.title: Cell lines that share a well are not independent observations in the Tahoe-100M drug screen
papers.abstract: Pooled drug screens treat and sequence dozens of cancer cell lines together in one well. Tahoe-100M, the largest, is used to train and benchmark models that predict how unmeasured cell lines respond to drugs, and its benchmarks, reproducibility ceilings and statistical tests treat the cell lines of a well, and random halves of a well's cells, as independent observations of a drug's effect. Because the drug is applied to the well, this is harmless only if the lines of a well share nothing beyond the drug's reproducible effect. We tested this with pairs of untreated control wells on 13 plates, with replicate wells whose labels we checked, and with two plates that repeat each other well by well. In each test the cell lines of a well share a component of expression that a replicate well does not reproduce, also when the two wells occupy the same inferred position; where drugs are present, it cannot be told apart from an interaction of plate and drug, but in untreated wells it can. In replicate wells at different positions whose labels pass the check, about a third of what two halves of a well have in common (35%, 95% interval 22-58%, 9 compounds) is not reproduced by the replicate well. The well effect inflates results that take something from a well and judge it in the same well: retrained versions of two published models that take a measured response as input lose about a quarter to a third of their score when the input comes from a replicate well instead of the predicted well (22-43% under the control-well reference), halves of a well overstate how well the experiment reproduces, and a test across the lines of a well calls 5 of 13 plates significant when two untreated wells are compared. Many labels of strongly responding replicate wells, those of plate 13 above all, fail the label check. Evaluations, ceilings and tests on such data should treat the well as the experimental unit.

papers.title: Accurate automated photo-identification of Near Eastern and European fire salamanders
papers.abstract: Photo-identification underpins non-invasive capture-recapture monitoring of amphibians, but manual identification becomes slow and error-prone as reference libraries grow. Focusing on the Near Eastern fire salamander (Salamandra infraimmaculata), we developed a pipeline based on zero-shot local-feature matching (SuperPoint and LightGlue) without species-specific training and evaluated it on $2{,}440$ field photographs from Haifa and Tel Dan in northern Israel. We isolated the yellow spot pattern, scored image similarity by the number of high-confidence keypoint matches, which reduced a confound whereby many-spotted individuals accumulate spurious matches, and assigned identities across the database by two-tier clustering. Pipeline-assisted expert review corrected misidentifications, reducing the number of identities by almost a quarter. On held-out individuals, the pipeline ranked the correct individual first for $95.2\%$ of queries and recovered identities with an ARI of $0.958$. Without modification, it reached $95.1\%$ and $91.7\%$ top-1 accuracy on two datasets of the European fire salamander (Salamandra salamandra) and recognised $93.7\%$ of recaptures in one of them, compared with $38$-$77\%$ for five established programs and $93.9\%$ for visual inspection. Zero-shot local-feature matching thus offers amphibian monitoring a re-identification tool that needs no training data, transfers between related species, scales to databases of over a thousand individuals, and can audit existing databases before capture-recapture analysis.

papers.title: Principled Human-AI Collaboration in Agentic Workflows
papers.abstract: Organizations adopting AI face the challenge of deciding which outputs can be released without human review while meeting the quality standards of human experts. We develop a statistical framework for delegating tasks between experts and black-box generate-verify workflows, in which AI-generated answers are verified and revised over multiple rounds. Before deployment, human experts evaluate selected outputs, and their judgments are used to calibrate the verifier threshold and number of attempts. Our method selects the policy with the highest estimated automation rate among statistically approved candidates, without modifying the generator or verifier. We establish finite-sample control of the error rate among released outputs, characterize the expert evaluations sufficient to attain a target automation rate, and derive a minimax lower bound establishing rate optimality in the quality margin and required confidence. In a MultiHiertt financial question-answering case study, average held-out automation increases from 2.50% to 24.17% as expert evaluations accumulate, while released-output error rates remain around 1.20%. In contrast, heuristics that release answers after consistently high verifier scores either violate the 5% error tolerance or automate at most 1.30% of tasks. Synthetic experiments further examine these theoretical predictions under controlled settings.

papers.title: From Tool State to Scientific Action: Auditing Decision Provenance in Biomedical Research Agents
papers.abstract: A scientific agent can give the same verdict while reading and citing different evidence. BioAgent-DF tests this separation using paired reference and candidate values saved at the same scientific computation site. It restores or transplants those values at their original coordinates, then runs the agent on healthy hardware. Across eight SciFact batches, Qwen3.5-4B shows repeatable citation changes in three capture-claim combinations, and Gemma 3 4B IT shows repeatable read and citation changes in four. These seven combinations cover two claims. Full restoration recovers the reference evidence sets while verdicts remain unchanged. Verdict changes observed under the baseline prompt did not recur under the explicit-example prompt. Complementary tool and optimizer experiments distinguish recovery of numerical state, recovery of ranked lists, and restoration of an agent's visible history. These results show that an audit should track both the evidence an agent uses and its final answer. In hERG cardiac-safety assay allocation, silent numerical faults changed testing decisions while the fixed-budget shortlist kept the same number of compounds labeled as blockers. After the agent had used faulty values, restoring its earlier execution state and supplying certified scores recovered all 39 changed decisions, whereas replacing the prediction file recovered none; no incorrect action was committed. A streaming implementation of the arithmetic checks reduced the total time for forward execution and verification by 42.4% relative to the original FP64 implementation, with identical flags and recovery outputs.

papers.title: A Debiased Machine Learning Single-Imputation Framework for Item Nonresponse in Surveys
papers.abstract: Machine-learning methods offer flexible alternatives to parametric models for imputing missing survey values. However, using their predictions in the customary imputed estimator does not automatically yield valid inference. We explain why the error from estimating the regression function can prevent root-$n$ consistency and develop inference for a finite population mean using a cross-fitted augmented inverse-probability-weighted (AIPW) estimator. The analysis combines an imputation model, a sampling design, and a missing-at-random response mechanism, while allowing dependence among sampling indicators. We establish double robustness and show that, under suitable regularity conditions, consistency of both nuisance estimators together with a product-rate condition yields oracle equivalence and asymptotic normality. We also derive consistent variance estimators accounting for sampling and nonresponse. To obtain a completed survey variable, we construct adjusted imputed values that preserve observed responses and whose weighted mean reproduces the AIPW estimate exactly. We further discuss aggregation of nuisance learners and the conditions under which it preserves the prediction rates needed for inference. Simulations show that cross-fitting can substantially reduce undercoverage, but may increase mean squared error when nuisance predictions are inaccurate.

papers.title: Transport for Conditional Sampling: Foundations and Applications
papers.abstract: Conditional sampling is central to Bayesian inference, generative modeling, and causal inference: given a joint law for random variables $X$ and $Y$ and an observation $Y=y$, one seeks to sample from the conditional law of $X\mid Y=y$. Even when the joint distribution is accurately represented, this task can be computationally difficult as it may require evaluating intractable normalizing constants or solving a new inference problem for each observation. Measure transport provides an approach to this problem by identifying a map with triangular structure that directly pushes forward a reference to the conditional of a joint distribution for any observation. This article reviews the theoretical, methodological, and algorithmic foundations of triangular transports, with the Knothe-Rosenblatt rearrangement as a canonical construction. We discuss methods for estimating triangular maps from finite samples, as well as their use in simulation-based inference and causal inference. While our primary aim is to review existing formulations, we also present new ideas and open questions for conditional sampling using transport.

papers.title: Measurement Error and Nonlinear Confounding: Structural Equation Modeling Versus Double Machine Learning
papers.abstract: A latent confounder measured by fallible indicators can be adjusted for with structural equation modeling (SEM), which corrects measurement error but requires a specified functional form, or with double machine learning (DML), which learns the form but ignores measurement error. We derive both population biases and the crossover reliability, the composite reliability above which DML with the indicators or their mean as inputs is less biased than linear SEM; it depends on the nonlinear share of confounding and falls when covariates predict the confounder. A 46-condition Monte Carlo study confirmed both biases and the predicted ordering. With gradient boosting, learning the conditional means raised the DML bias by up to 0.05 and moved the finite-sample crossover upward. A quadratic SEM was unbiased when its form was correct and removed two thirds of the linear-SEM bias under a saturating nonlinearity but little of it under a cubic one.

papers.title: FACET: Feasibility-Automaton Complete Enumeration and Truncation-Free Scoring of Molecular Formulas from MS/MS
papers.abstract: Determining the neutral molecular formula of a precursor ion from its tandem mass (MS/MS) spectrum is the first step in identifying an unknown small molecule. Existing methods trade recall, whether the correct formula is among the candidates, against the cost of examining each candidate. Methods that examine each candidate in depth must first shorten the list, by limiting element counts or truncating it, and that is where the correct formula is lost. End-to-end regressors are fast but guarantee neither validity nor recall. We present FACET, which separates deciding which formulas to consider from deciding which one to choose. A feasibility automaton builds a formula one element count at a time and admits exactly the formulas that fit the precursor mass and satisfy the ring-and-double-bond and valence constraints. Run as an exhaustive search, it enumerates the complete feasible set, so every candidate is valid and recall is fixed by the chemical constraints rather than by a trained model. A small neural scoring head then ranks every feasible formula from one pass of a pretrained spectrum encoder, so no candidate is discarded. On the NPLIB1 benchmark FACET reaches top-1 accuracies of $0.859$ with the adduct known and $0.729$ with it unknown, compared with $0.766$ and $0.660$ for the strongest established method, and its recall is the highest. On the external CASMI 2022 set its recall is $1.000$, and with the adduct unknown it is the most accurate of the methods compared.

papers.title: Sentiment sensing: comparative analysis of multilingual sentiment dynamics
papers.abstract: Cross-country sentiment analysis faces three fundamental challenges: language-specific biases distort comparisons, compositional data constraints invalidate standard statistics and temporal dynamics lack rigorous testing frameworks. We introduce sentiment sensing, a framework that addresses these gaps through integrated statistical methods. By combining compositional data analysis, functional data methods, and non-parametric inference, sentiment sensing enables valid multilingual comparisons and statistically defensible detection of sentiment shifts. Our framework has been tested in two case studies, analyzing news articles from the 27 countries of the European Union on the topics of energy and artificial intelligence. Sentiment sensing focuses on multilingual sentiment analysis enabling rigorous comparative science.
